headline: Hiring struggles. Nuclear tests. Budget boosts.
deck: The space industry grapples with workforce challenges while funding flows.

stories.head: Space industry faces workforce conundrum
stories.body: The space sector is contemplating ambitious hiring to tackle its historic labor shortages, with some companies reporting difficulty in finding qualified personnel. This comes as the industry prepares for an influx of projects, but as one industry insider quipped, finding a rocket scientist might be easier than finding a unicorn. The demand for talent is at an all-time high, yet the supply remains stubbornly low.
stories.soWhat: If you thought recruiting was tough now, wait until the next wave of launches begins.

stories.head: Nuclear batteries get a test drive in orbit
stories.body: A startup is currently testing nuclear battery technology in orbit, aiming to provide a reliable power source for satellites that can't rely on solar energy. This initiative is a bold move, especially given the historical hesitance around nuclear tech in space. If successful, it could mean a significant shift in how we power our satellites, especially in shadowed regions of space.
stories.soWhat: If this works, it might just light up the competition for satellite power sources.

stories.head: Space resilience funding sees a hefty boost
stories.body: The FY27 budget markup has added $1.4 billion to the space resilience line, signaling a serious commitment to bolstering national security in space. This increase highlights the growing recognition that space is not just an afterthought but a critical domain requiring substantial investment. As the stakes rise, so too does the funding.
stories.soWhat: It turns out the final frontier isn't just for exploration; it's a budget battleground.

talent.statLabel: Job orders YoY · plus 2 starters per head, an 8-year first
talent.head: Demand has doubled. So has our hit rate.
talent.body: EVONA's job orders are up 2.0× year-over-year, and for the first time in our eight-year history we're placing two new starters per EVONA staff member. The first number says demand is real. The second says we're converting it, which in recruitment is the only number that actually matters. Growth is heaviest in Series B/C startups; primes are running flat. Compensation isn't the variable. The constraint is schedule risk in the primes: senior engineers leave Boeing, Lockheed, Northrop because they want to ship hardware before retirement.
